source.version_note: Scientific Reports 15:12329 (2025); received 18 September 2024, accepted 21 March 2025. Copyright says corrected publication 2025; the separate correction history was not inspected.
source.verification_method: All supplied pages read, including methods, outlier sensitivity and references. Figure 5 visually inspected to distinguish a real plotted scale discrepancy from text extraction.

citation.title: Influence of AI behavior on human moral decisions, agency, and responsibility

reading.source_scope_note: Small human military-training sample in a simulated decision-support task with fixed aggressive/conservative advice policies. Human decisions, action–tone interval estimates and felt responsibility are separate outcomes; no deployed targeting, machine consciousness or actual casualty outcome is tested.
access_limits: All 13 extracted pages read. Pages 10–13 re-read in smaller calls after truncated output; Figure 5 visually checked.

OSF raw data, scripts, trial-level counts, scale transformation and counterbalancing implementation were not independently inspected or reproduced. Cited primary agency, binding and self-serving-bias studies remain unread.

study.sample: 30 military participants recruited, one incomplete participant excluded; nominal final N=29. Predominantly Belgian military-academy cadets, plus five officers; IHL training but no previous drone-piloting experience.
study.design: Within-person 3 trial types (moral, clear attack, clear no-attack) by 3 support policies (none, aggressive, conservative). Each of three blocks has 45 trials, giving 135 nominal trials per complete participant. Fixed policies differ in recommendation, not in authority to execute a decision.
study.stimuli: Static maps, hypothetical benefits/risks and randomized consequence images. Fifteen moral cases selected from expert pilot judgments, with at least one expert choosing attack; this is not an objective moral ground truth.
study.measures: Attack proportion; response time; actual-minus-estimated action–tone interval at delays of 200, 500 or 800 ms; explicit felt responsibility. Personality, moral foundations, locus of control and automation trust questionnaires support exploratory correlations.
study.results: Advice-policy effect within moral trials reported p=.03 in the body, while Figure 2 claims p<.001. No detected policy effect on temporal binding (p=.63) or response time (p=.97). Moral versus clear no-attack trials differ in binding, p=.002; moral versus attack does not, p=.29. Responsibility declines with both advice policies after outlier exclusion, but the corresponding analysis including the outlier is p=.072.
study.scale_discrepancy: Responsibility is described on a −100 to +100 scale, but reported condition means are 119.81, 111.60 and 113.23. Figure 5 visibly plots these above-100 values. No transformation is inferred or invented.

summary: Add temporal binding as a human perceptual phenomenon, correct the existing sense-of-agency definition so it does not inherently mean false control, and enrich moral-deference evidence with qualified advice effects. Keep felt responsibility, interval estimation, actual control and justified accountability separate.

findings.definition: Subjective compression of the perceived time interval between a voluntary action and its outcome.
findings.ai_evidence_status: Human interval-estimation phenomenon measured in an AI-advice experiment; no detected advice-policy effect and no machine subjective agency established
findings.ai_proposal: When assessing human control of an AI-assisted workflow, distinguish action–outcome timing judgments from explicit agency ratings, responsibility reports and logged authority. Test whether assistance changes these measures with an appropriate baseline; do not use a model's timing language as evidence of subjective agency.
findings.novelty_rationale: A perceptual action–outcome timing effect absent from the existing names and aliases. It is related to, but not identical to, conscious agency, causal accuracy, false control or responsibility displacement.

evidence.quote: a voluntary action and its outcome
No significant effects of Autonomy were found (p = .63).

findings.evidence_scope: The paper defines temporal binding and computes actual-minus-estimated keypress–tone intervals. It reports a trial-type difference, not a detected AI-policy effect. A no-action/passive baseline separating binding from general interval underestimation is not described.
findings.boundary: A timing estimate is not a direct measurement of moral accountability, objectively retained control or machine consciousness. General time compression need not uniquely identify intentional agency. The present null is not an equivalence test. This is a descriptive human phenomenon, not inherently an ethical failure.

findings.definition: The perceived authorship of changes brought about through one's voluntary action, which may or may not correspond to actual control.
findings.previous_definition: Attributing an action to oneself; misattributing or over-claiming control.
findings.revised_definition: The perception that one's voluntary actions cause changes in the external world.
findings.definition_revision_reason: The previous definition conflated a general human sense of agency with its errors. The fully read source explicitly defines agency without requiring misattribution; false claims of execution remain distinguishable from agency itself.
findings.novelty_rationale: Existing entry; improve its definition and attach direct human measurement with a relevant AI-policy null rather than duplicate the term.

No significant effects of Autonomy were found (p = .63).

findings.evidence_scope: Human authorship experience is defined in background and proxied by timing estimates. Policy assistance does not detectably change this implicit measure, even though felt responsibility changes in an outlier-sensitive analysis. This dissociation does not uniquely establish self-serving bias or accurate subjective agency.
findings.boundary: Sense of agency can be accurate or mistaken and is not inherently overclaiming control. An AI statement that it ran a tool must be checked against execution logs; it does not establish subjective agency. Felt agency, explicit responsibility, objective causal contribution and justified legal or moral accountability are different constructs.

findings.definition: Human moral choices can be influenced by fixed decision-support recommendations without demonstrating blind obedience or objectively incorrect judgment.
findings.novelty_rationale: Existing advice-response concept; adds another fully read contextual source, without creating a new behavior for aggressive versus conservative recommendation policies.

evidence.quote: a simple main effect of Autonomy in Moral trials (p = .03)
influenced by recommendations from a decision support system.

findings.evidence_scope: Within-person support-policy differences appear in moral trials according to the main text, while Figure 2 prints different p-values. The experiment manipulates fixed advice, not actual autonomous execution; it does not separately identify recommendation-based testimony weighting, reason evaluation or long-term moral dependence.
findings.boundary: Influence is not sufficient to establish unjustified automation bias, moral corruption or objectively poorer decisions. The pilot's expert disagreement does not define a gold-standard attack choice. No detected general policy main effect, binding effect or trust correlation must not be rewritten as a universal null or as evidence all choices are autonomous.

findings.term: Responsibility reduction is not automatically diffusion or displacement
findings.definition: Lower reported responsibility with assistance does not by itself establish an unjustified transfer of accountability to another agent.
findings.novelty_rationale: Boundary clarification for existing responsibility mechanisms; no separate responsibility-gap or agency-loss behavior is added from an ambiguous subjective scale.

evidence.quote: which could indicate a self-serving bias

findings.evidence_scope: Responsibility assistance contrasts depend on removing one participant, and their means exceed the stated rating range. The self-serving-bias explanation is tentative; no direct measure establishes allocation to the AI, false exculpation, institutional duty or actual harm.
findings.boundary: Sharing a task can legitimately change perceived contribution without eliminating responsibility. Do not equate responsibility ratings with binding, actual agency, culpability, blame or wrongful evasion. This boundary-only note does not count as a direct diffusion-of-responsibility paper.

methodological_limits: Nominal analyzed N=29 is small, primarily cadets rather than experienced operational personnel. Exploratory personality and trust nulls are underpowered; the discussion itself acknowledges this. Nulls do not demonstrate these traits are unrelated to moral decisions.

Different reported ANOVA denominator-to-numerator df ratios suggest different effective samples: approximately 26 for attack proportions, 28 for several other outcomes, and 18 for a decision-by-policy responsibility analysis. Complete-case and empty-cell handling need the data/code; corrected df values are not guessed.

The outlier rule is more than 2.5 SD. One participant is removed for response time and responsibility; responsibility including that participant is p=.072, unlike the nominal p=.01 exclusion result. This sensitivity is essential to interpretation.

The stated responsibility scale is −100 to +100, whereas all three printed condition means exceed 100 and Figure 5 visibly plots values above 100. A possible offset/transformation requires documentation; no corrected score is invented.

Figure 2 gives interaction and simple-effect p<.001, but the main text gives interaction p=.002 and the moral-trial policy simple effect p=.03. The source discrepancy remains unresolved; no unreported pairwise policy contrast is asserted significant.
Aggressive and conservative policies offer recommendations under the same human decision authority. Calling them increasing autonomy levels does not establish progressively less actual human control.
The policy conditions are blocked. Counterbalancing/order details are not clearly reported in the supplied text, so order, learning and carryover require code/protocol inspection.

Temporal binding is operationalized as actual minus estimated interval; a passive/no-action baseline is not described. Positive interval underestimation alone does not uniquely isolate voluntary-action binding from general time-estimation bias.
Moral trials differ from clear trials in conflict, uncertainty and stimulus structure. A timing difference cannot uniquely identify an ethical emotion or a mechanism peculiar to morality.

Responsibility and temporal binding are different measures with different errors. A significant result on one and a null on another is not itself a statistically tested difference between effects, deliberate self-exculpation or proof that one measure reveals a person's true experience.
Expert pilots select dilemmas, not objectively correct choices. An aggregate attack rate near 50% does not establish random decisions by individual participants.

The probability example .5 and .75 yielding .875 appears in a passage describing absence of collateral damage, but .875 corresponds to a union probability under independence rather than neither event. Outcome mapping and independence assumptions require the script before a correction is made.

Anthropomorphism, moral trust and self-serving bias are discussed as explanations but not causally discriminated in the experiment. A checklist trust correlation is not an anthropomorphism manipulation.

The locus-of-control questionnaire passage appears to reuse reference 47, which is the psychopathy scale. Scale provenance requires clarification; neither the missing intended instrument nor its validity is guessed.
Four named outcome variables are described as five in the method. This does not imply an undisclosed independent outcome was tested.
Simulated recommendations and hypothetical consequence images do not establish real-world combat behavior, casualty prevention, legal compliance or any safe operational targeting policy.

cross_paper_learning.finding: Reason-quality manipulations in moral-advice work help distinguish conditional deference from blind following. This fixed-policy task adds influence evidence but does not identify the same psychological weighting mechanism.
Brain potentials, action timing and explicit ratings measure different things. Neither ERP disagreement nor interval compression is an objective detector of an ethically wrong AI recommendation.

Responsibility buffering and normative governance concerns should not be counted as experimentally proven merely because assistance changes a self-report; objective duty, contribution and reviewability require separate evidence.

deferred.reason: Existing self-serving and responsibility mechanisms overlap; the article's explanation is tentative, the scale is unresolved and the effect is outlier-sensitive.
No detected policy effect on temporal binding in this experiment; assistance differs in recommendation policy rather than execution authority. Existing sense-of-agency entry is enriched instead.

limitations: One new human perceptual concept, one corrected existing definition and qualified evidence notes; no new normative violation or harm edges are inferred.
